Sara - CS: Hey team, heads-up: NimblePay just escalated — seeing intermittent 429s and large p99 latency spikes during short bursts of traffic. They say it feels like throttling even though their quota isn't near the daily limit. They pasted a few headers from responses:

User sample headers:
```
x-request-id: ab12cd34
x-rate-limit-limit: 120
x-rate-limit-remaining: 0
x-rate-limit-reset: 30
x-kv-cache-hit: false
x-model: redwood-3b
```

Customer claims pattern: low steady traffic, then 10–30 reqs/sec burst for ~15s => many 429s and some responses taking 2-3s. They are on hosted tier, not Dedicated. Any quick triage steps?

Nina - Runtime: Thanks Sara. Two quick possibilities: 1) Per-key concurrency / per-customer burst protection (not just daily quota) and 2) continuous batching + KV cache cold starts causing short compute spikes and queueing. Both can look like "throttling" at the app layer.

Matt - Eng: Repro checklist we usually ask for: exact curl with headers, a request-id from a 429, and a short timeline (timestamps). If they can run a small repro script that fires bursts, we can capture server-side metrics (concurrency, queue length, batch sizes).

Sara - CS: I asked for a curl and they sent this quick repro they ran from staging: 
```
for i in {1..50}; do curl -s -i -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"prompt":"x", "max_tokens":512}' &
done
wait
```
They said about 20/50 returned 429s, others were 200 but some were 2.5s.

Oliver - SRE: Can confirm that pattern: when many short-lived requests all hit around the same time we can see a burst of batches being flushed and many backend slots occupied. If per-API-key concurrency is N (say 16), bursts >N will queue and some client retry/backoff logic can amplify retries and cause more 429s. Also KV cache hits matter — if many requests are for new prefixes we pay full compute per-request.

Nina - Runtime: Steps for customer to differentiate quota vs concurrency vs cache effects: 
1) Check rate-limit headers: x-rate-limit-remaining and x-rate-limit-reset. If remaining is zero at time of 429, it's quota. If remaining >0 but you still see 429s, it's concurrency or short-term per-key burst throttling.
2) Look at x-kv-cache-hit (we added that header) — lots of false/false means cache misses, expect higher compute per-request.
3) Ask them to run the same script but with a tiny stagger (sleep 10ms between starts) or reduce parallelism to 8 and see if 429s disappear.

Matt - Eng: Also check client behavior — many SDKs do immediate retries on 429 without jitter which worsens the burst. Recommend exponential backoff with jitter e.g.:
```
retry_delay = base * 2**attempt + random(0, jitter_ms)
```
And honor Retry-After header if present.

Sara - CS: NimblePay says they use our official SDK with default retries. They rely on low latency so they prefer smaller retries. They're nervous about increasing delays.

Kevin - Product: Quick product note: we surface per-key concurrency and short-window burst metrics in the Console, but it's easy to miss. Sara, please ask them to share the Console screenshot for the event window. We should consider a tooltip explaining burst headroom.

Nina - Runtime: For immediate mitigations we can offer: 
- Temporarily increase their per-key concurrency limit (manual throttle bump) if they have legitimate short bursts and it's safe.
- Advise changing batch configuration client-side: lower batch_max_tokens or lower batch_timeout_ms so batches flush earlier and reduce peak memory/compute per-batch.
- Encourage enabling prefix/KV caching where applicable or warming the cache by sending a small warmup set before bursts.

Oliver - SRE: I've looked at server logs around thread_ts 1718502000 for their customer id — saw a spike in batch size mean from 6->18 during the burst window and concurrent inflight requests hitting the per-key cap. I can manually bump headroom for a 1-hour window while we investigate if support approves.

Sara - CS: Customer approved a temporary bump, can you apply +8 concurrency for 1 hour? Also requested a clear repro plan so they can tune their client.

Oliver - SRE: Will do. Applied and watching — so far p99 latency dropped to ~550ms and 429s stopped in the short test. Please advise them to run the staggered and reduced-parallelism tests to confirm.

Matt - Eng: Long-term fixes we should recommend to customers and maybe bake into SDK defaults: 
- Respect Retry-After and use jittered exponential backoff.
- Prefer pacing bursts via client-side queue/token-bucket to avoid synchronized spikes.
- Use smaller streaming chunks or progressive responses for low-latency UX rather than many parallel full-size generation requests.

Nina - Runtime: Note on KV cache: we saw customers hit poor perceived throttling when their requests had highly variable prefixes (session IDs, timestamps in prompt). That kills cache hit ratio. Recommend normalizing prompts or moving dynamic data to metadata fields if possible. Also consider enabling prefix-only cache mode for certain routes.

Sara - CS: I sent NimblePay a step-by-step repro plan: 1) run their current burst script (50 parallel) and capture x-request-id for 429s; 2) run the staggered-version (sleep 10ms) and compare 429 rate; 3) run with reduced parallelism (8) and measure; 4) check Console per-key concurrency graph and KV hit ratio. Asking them to paste 2 x-request-ids back here.

deploy-bot: deploy succeeded: runtime/feature/cache-metrics v2.3.1 promoted to hosted region eu-west-1 :rocket: 

Nina - Runtime: If they provide a request-id we can pull a detailed trace (batch composition, KV hits, allocation timing). If persists after our config suggestions we should escalate to on-call runtime for deeper kernel/queue analysis.

Sara - CS: Great, customer will run tests and share request-ids. I'll update thread when they reply. Thanks all :pray:
